mainTopic: Is a סימן that is likely to be trampled still a valid סימן? רבה and רבא each read the ברייתא of כריכות and אלומות in their own way, and the גמרא then challenges רבה from the משנה of loaves of bread.
overview: This amud continues the argument between רבה and רבא about a סימן העשוי לידרס, a sign likely to be trampled. רבה says it does not count, and רבא says it does. First רבה and רבא each read the ברייתא about bundles and sheaves their own way, so that ברייתא proves nothing. Next the גמרא tries to refute רבה from the משנה, which requires announcing a homeowner's loaves even in a public area. רבה answers that people don't step on food, and his answer survives the challenges about גוים and animals. Then the גמרא asks whether the argument between the תנא קמא and רבי יהודה in the משנה matches the argument of רבה and רבא. In two versions, רב זביד in the name of רבא shows that the תנאים really argue only about a סימן הבא מאיליו, a sign that came by accident. רבה can read the משנה that way too. The amud ends with practical rulings: saying 'woe for my money loss' counts as יאוש, bundles without a סימן are kept or announced depending on the place and how they lie, and an item with a סימן must always be announced.

steps.title: רבה finishes reading the ברייתא through signs
steps.stepSummary: רבה explains the ברייתא based on his view: small bundles in a public area get trampled, so their sign is lost. In a private area they are not trampled. Tall sheaves are never trampled.
steps.simpleTranslation: Small bundles in a public area belong to the finder, because they get trampled. In a private area he takes them and announces, because they are not trampled. Sheaves, in either kind of area, he takes and announces, since they stand tall and are not trampled.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes showing how רבה reads the ברייתא so that it fits his view that a sign likely to be trampled does not count.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבה, everything depends on whether the sign survives. Small bundles in a busy public place get stepped on, so their sign is treated as already gone, and the finder keeps them. In a private place, or with tall sheaves anywhere, the sign stays whole, so the finder must announce.

Large, tall sheaves of grain

A private or quiet area

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבה's reading of the ברייתא, which began before this section.

steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא fits רבה: a sign that gets trampled is not a sign.

steps.title: רבא reads the same ברייתא through location
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains the same ברייתא as being about location as the sign. Small bundles in a public area get kicked and roll away, so their location tells you nothing. Heavy sheaves stay where they were put.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא explains it his way, as being about location. Small bundles in a public area belong to the finder, because they get kicked and roll away. In a private area he must announce, because they don't roll. Sheaves, in either area, he takes and announces, since they are heavy and don't roll.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives his own reading of the same ברייתא, so it does not prove רבה right.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבא, the 'sign' in the ברייתא is the place where the item was left. In a public area, small bundles get kicked around, so the place no longer identifies them. Heavy sheaves don't move, so their location still works as a sign. This way the ברייתא says nothing about trampled signs.

keyTerms.meaning: He explains it according to his own view
Location, used as an identifying sign
It gets kicked and rolls away
They are heavy

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא can be read two ways: רבה reads it as about signs that get trampled, and רבא reads it as about location that gets lost when things roll. So it proves nothing for either side.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Reading the ברייתא as being about location as a sign
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא fits רבא too, so it does not decide the argument.

steps.title: Proof from the homeowner's loaves refutes רבה
steps.stepSummary: The משנה says a baker's loaves belong to the finder. So a homeowner's loaves must be announced, because each homeowner's bread looks different. Since the משנה makes no difference between public and private areas, a sign likely to be trampled still counts. That refutes רבה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: a baker's loaves belong to the finder. So a homeowner's loaves must be announced. Why? Because they have a sign: everyone knows what each person's bread looks like. And the משנה makes no difference between a public area and a private area; he takes and announces. So a sign that is likely to be trampled is a sign. This refutes רבה!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof from the משנה that a sign likely to be trampled does count. This is a strong attack on רבה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה only says a baker's loaves belong to the finder, so a homeowner's loaves must be announced. A homeowner's bread has a recognizable shape, which is its sign. Since the משנה does not limit this to private areas, it must apply even in a public area where the loaves could be stepped on. That goes against רבה.

steps.kashyaTarget: רבה's view that סימן העשוי לידרס is not a sign
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A homeowner's loaves must be announced even in a public area, where they could be trampled. So their sign counts even though it might be trampled.

steps.title: רבה: people don't step over food
steps.stepSummary: רבה answers that loaves are different: people don't pass by food and step on it. So the loaves' sign is not likely to be trampled at all.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה can tell you: there, the reason is that people don't pass over food.
steps.whatsHappening: רבה defends himself. The loaves are not a case of a sign likely to be trampled, because people don't step on food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה agrees the loaves must be announced, but not because a trampled sign counts. Since people treat food with respect and won't walk over it, bread in a public area is not expected to be trampled. Its sign is safe, so the case doesn't touch his rule.

keyTerms.meaning: He could tell you: introduces a defense
There, in that case
One does not pass over food (without picking it up)

steps.whyThisMatters: This shows how a case can be pulled out of a rule's reach: the loaves are not really 'likely to be trampled,' so they don't test רבה's view.

phrases.english: Rabba could tell you:
There, this is the reason:
because people do not pass over food.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Different reason: the case is not actually one of a sign likely to be trampled
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The loaves showed that a sign likely to be trampled still counts.
steps.terutzMaskana: Loaves are not likely to be trampled, because people respect food.

steps.title: But non-Jews might trample them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: גוים don't keep this custom of respecting food, so they might step on the loaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there are non-Jews!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רבה's answer: not everyone avoids stepping on food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה's answer depends on everyone respecting food. גוים passing through a public area would not keep this custom, so the loaves could still get trampled.

keyTerms.meaning: But there is: introduces a challenge

phrases.english: But there are non-Jews!

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: גוים don't hold back from stepping on food, so the sign could still be trampled.

steps.title: Non-Jews fear sorcery
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that גוים worry the loaves were left there for witchcraft, so they keep away from them.
steps.simpleTranslation: Non-Jews are worried about sorcery.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that גוים also stay away from the loaves, for a different reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bread lying in the road looks to גוים like part of a magic spell, so they avoid touching or stepping on it. So the loaves still won't be trampled.

keyTerms.meaning: They are worried

phrases.english: Non-Jews are worried about sorcery.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Factual answer: גוים also avoid the bread
steps.terutzMaskana: גוים won't trample the loaves either.

steps.title: But animals and dogs might trample them
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects again: animals and dogs don't care about respect or sorcery, and they could trample the loaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: But there are animals and dogs!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רבה's answer once more, this time with animals.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even if all people avoid the loaves, animals and dogs roaming a public area would step on them. So the sign is still likely to be trampled.

keyTerms.meaning: Animals, livestock
Dogs

phrases.english: But there are animals and dogs!

steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that loaves in a public area won't be trampled
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Animals don't hold back from food, so the loaves could still be trampled.

steps.title: A place without animals and dogs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the משנה is talking about a place where animals and dogs are not common. So רבה's defense stands.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is talking about a place where animals and dogs are not common.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the case of the משנה to a place without many animals, which keeps רבה's answer working.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the loaves are found where animals and dogs rarely pass, nothing is likely to trample them. So the משנה's rule about homeowner's loaves never involves a sign likely to be trampled, and רבה is not refuted.

keyTerms.meaning: A place

steps.whatToRemember: רבה survives the challenge from the loaves: in the case of the משנה, the loaves are not likely to be trampled. People respect food, גוים fear sorcery, and the place has few animals. So the משנה tells us nothing about a sign that really is likely to be trampled.

phrases.english: In a place where animals and dogs are not common.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case: the משנה is talking about a place with few animals
steps.terutzMaskana: The loaves won't be trampled there, so רבה's view stands.

steps.title: Maybe this is an older argument between תנאים
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests the רבה/רבא argument matches a dispute in the משנה: רבי יהודה requires announcing an item with something unusual inside it, which implies the תנא קמא lets the finder keep it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this is like a dispute of תנאים. רבי יהודה says: any item that has something unusual about it must be announced. How so? If he found a round fig cake with a clay shard inside it, or a loaf with coins inside it. This implies that the תנא קמא holds that these belong to the finder.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is setting up a possible link between the argument of רבה and רבא and a dispute in the משנה. It quotes רבי יהודה and shows that the תנא קמא must disagree with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה says something unusual inside an item, like a shard or coins, works as a סימן, so the finder must announce it. The תנא קמא did not list these items among the things to announce, so he must hold the finder keeps them. The next step will try to figure out what exactly they are arguing about.

steps.title: They must be arguing about a sign likely to be trampled
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא assumes both תנאים agree that an accidental sign counts and that people pass over food. So it suggests they argue about a sign likely to be trampled, just like רבה and רבא.
steps.simpleTranslation: They assumed that everyone agrees a sign that comes by itself counts as a sign, and that people pass over food. So isn't it that they argue about a sign likely to be trampled? One master holds it is not a sign, and the other master holds it is a sign.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains how the תנאים could be arguing about the same thing as רבה and רבא. It rules out two other possible reasons for their argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two points are assumed to be agreed by all. First, a sign that got there by accident still counts. Second, people do walk past food, so a loaf can get stepped on. The only issue left is whether a sign that will probably get trampled still counts. On that view the תנא קמא sides with רבה (not a sign) and רבי יהודה sides with רבא (a sign).

steps.title: The תנא קמא himself requires announcing a homeowner's loaves
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד in the name of רבא rejects the suggestion. If the תנא קמא held that a trampled-type sign does not count and that people step over food, he would not require announcing loaves found in a public place.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבא: if you think the תנא קמא holds that a sign likely to be trampled is not a sign, and that people pass over food, then why must one announce a homeowner's loaves found in a public area?
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד pushes back on the suggestion from step 10. He points to a ruling of the תנא קמא that does not fit it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, the תנא קמא rules that a homeowner's loaves must be announced. If people step over food and a trampled-type sign does not count, the sign on those loaves would be worthless and no announcement would be needed. So the תנא קמא cannot hold both ideas together.

steps.title: The real argument is about a sign that came by itself
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד explains that everyone agrees a trampled-type sign counts. The תנא קמא and רבי יהודה argue only about an accidental sign, like a shard or coins that fell in.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב זביד said in the name of רבא: everyone holds that a sign likely to be trampled is a sign, and that people pass over food. Here they argue about a sign that came by itself. The תנא קמא holds that a sign that came by itself is not a sign, and רבי יהודה holds that it is a sign.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד offers a new explanation of the dispute between the תנאים. Their argument has nothing to do with רבה and רבא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier assumption is flipped. Now the trampled-type sign is agreed by everyone to count, which explains why the תנא קמא requires announcing the loaves. The point of argument is an accidental sign. The תנא קמא says a shard or coins that fell in by chance cannot identify the owner, and רבי יהודה says they can.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather: replaces the earlier explanation with a new one

steps.title: How רבה explains the dispute in the משנה
steps.stepSummary: רבה says everyone agrees a trampled-type sign does not count and people do not pass over food. The תנא קמא and רבי יהודה argue only about an accidental sign.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה can tell you: everyone agrees that a sign likely to be trampled is not a sign, and that people do not walk past food. Here they argue about a sign that came by itself. The תנא קמא holds it is not a sign, and רבי יהודה holds it is a sign.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד just explained the משנה in a way that fits רבא. Now the גמרא shows that רבה can also explain the משנה so that it fits his own view.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבה keeps his rule that a סימן העשוי לידרס does not count. He avoids the problem of the loaves by adding that אין מעבירין על האוכלין. Someone will pick up the bread before it gets trampled, so its sign survives. That leaves the argument in the משנה to be only about a סימן הבא מאיליו.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
A sign that is likely to be trampled and wiped out
People do not walk past food; they pick it up
A sign that came about by itself, by accident

And here they argue about a sign that came by itself.

phrases.aramaic: תַּנָּא קַמָּא סָבַר: לָא הָוֵי סִימָן,
phrases.english: The first תנא holds: it is not a sign,
and רבי יהודה holds: it is a sign.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallels רב זביד's explanation in step 12, but shows how רבה's view also fits the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Relocating the dispute to a different issue while adding an assumption about food
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to support רבא against רבה.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבה can read the משנה as agreeing with him, with the argument only about a סימן הבא מאיליו.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows the משנה cannot decide between רבה and רבא, because each can read it his own way.

steps.title: Another version: maybe they argue about passing over food
steps.stepSummary: In another version, the Sages assumed everyone agrees an accidental sign counts and a trampled-type sign does not. So they suggested the תנאים argue about whether people pass over food.
steps.simpleTranslation: Some say the Sages assumed that everyone agrees a sign that came by itself is a sign, and a sign likely to be trampled is not a sign. If so, don't they argue about whether people walk past food? One holds people walk past it, and the other holds they do not.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of the discussion. Here the suggestion is that the תנאים argue about whether people pass over food.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If both sides agree about the two kinds of signs, something else must explain why the תנא קמא lets the finder keep some items. The suggestion is that the תנא קמא holds מעבירין, so food would get trampled and lose its sign. רבי יהודה holds אין מעבירין, so the sign survives.

keyTerms.meaning: Some say; another version of the discussion
They assumed
Isn't it that...? (introduces a suggestion)
People walk past food and leave it
One Sage... and the other Sage

steps.confusionAlert: This is a new version (איכא דאמרי), not a continuation of רבה's answer. Both versions assume a סימן הבא מאיליו counts. They differ on the second assumption. The first version (step 10) assumed everyone agrees מעבירין על האוכלין. This version assumes everyone agrees a סימן העשוי לידרס is not a sign, so the suggested dispute moves to whether people pass over food.

phrases.english: Some say: they assumed

phrases.aramaic: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא סִימָן הַבָּא מֵאֵילָיו הָוֵי סִימָן,
phrases.english: that everyone agrees a sign that came by itself is a sign,

phrases.aramaic: וְסִימָן הֶעָשׂוּי לִידָּרֵס לָא הָוֵי סִימָן.
phrases.english: and a sign likely to be trampled is not a sign.

phrases.aramaic: מַאי לָאו: בְּמַעֲבִירִין עַל הָאוֹכָלִין קָא מִיפַּלְגִי,
phrases.english: Isn't it that they argue about whether people walk past food?
One Sage holds: people walk past it,
and the other Sage holds: people do not walk past it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a second version of the analysis of the תנאים dispute in step 9, using different assumptions.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What is the real point of argument between the תנא קמא and רבי יהודה?

steps.title: The loaves in a public place disprove the suggestion
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד in the name of רבא says the תנא קמא cannot hold that a trampled-type sign does not count and that people pass over food. If he did, why would loaves found in a public place need announcing?
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבא: If you think the תנא קמא holds that a sign likely to be trampled is not a sign, and that people walk past food, then why must someone announce a homeowner's loaves found in a public place?
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד rejects the suggestion from the last step. He uses the case of loaves in the משנה, which the תנא קמא says must be announced.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a public place, loaves left lying there would be trampled if people walk past food. Under the suggested view, that kind of sign would not count, so the finder should keep the loaves. But the תנא קמא requires announcing them, so he cannot hold both of these ideas.

keyTerms.meaning: If you think that...
A homeowner's loaves, which have a recognizable look
A public area
He announces the found item

phrases.english: רב זביד said in the name of רבא:

phrases.aramaic: אִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ סָבַר תַּנָּא קַמָּא
phrases.english: If you think the first תנא holds

phrases.aramaic: סִימָן הֶעָשׂוּי לִידָּרֵס לָא הָוֵי סִימָן,
phrases.english: that a sign likely to be trampled is not a sign,
and that people walk past food,

phrases.aramaic: כִּכָּרוֹת שֶׁל בַּעַל הַבַּיִת בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
phrases.english: then for a homeowner's loaves found in a public area,
why does he announce them?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא: אִי סָלְקָא דַעְתָּךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion of step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The idea that the תנא קמא holds both that a trampled-type sign does not count and that people pass over food.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It conflicts with the תנא קמא's ruling that loaves found in a public place must be announced.

steps.title: רב זביד's conclusion: they argue only about an accidental sign
steps.stepSummary: Everyone agrees a trampled-type sign counts and that people pass over food. The argument is only about a sign that came by itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב זביד said in the name of רבא: everyone holds that a sign likely to be trampled is a sign, and that people walk past food. Here they argue about a sign that came by itself. The תנא קמא holds it is not a sign, and רבי יהודה holds it is a sign.
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting the suggestion, רב זביד gives the correct explanation of the dispute in the משנה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Because a trampled-type sign counts, the loaves must be announced even if people walk past them. So the only open question between the תנאים is whether an accidental sign, like a shard or coins that fell in, counts.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (introduces the corrected explanation)
They hold
It counts as a sign

steps.whatToRemember: In both versions, the תנא קמא and רבי יהודה argue only about a סימן הבא מאיליו. The משנה does not settle the argument about a סימן העשוי לידרס.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב זְבִיד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא:
phrases.english: Rather, רב זביד said in the name of רבא:

phrases.aramaic: דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא סָבְרִי סִימָן הֶעָשׂוּי לִידָּרֵס –
phrases.english: Everyone holds that a sign likely to be trampled
is a sign,
and that people walk past food.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָכָא בְּסִימָן הַבָּא מֵאֵילָיו קָא מִיפַּלְגִי,
phrases.english: And here they argue about a sign that came by itself.

phrases.aramaic: דְּתַנָּא קַמָּא סָבַר: סִימָן הַבָּא מֵאֵילָיו –
phrases.english: The first תנא holds that a sign that came by itself
is not a sign,
and רבי יהודה holds: it is a sign.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רַב זְבִיד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the correct explanation after the rejection in step 15.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The תנאים argue about whether people pass over food.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone agrees a trampled-type sign counts and that people pass over food. They argue only about a סימן הבא מאיליו.

steps.title: רבה's way of explaining the argument in the second version
steps.stepSummary: רבה says everyone agrees that a trampled-type sign does not count and that people do not pass over food. The argument is only about a sign that came by itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבה would tell you: everyone agrees that a sign likely to be trampled is not a real sign, and that people do not walk past food. Here they argue about a sign that came by itself. The תנא קמא holds it is not a sign, and רבי יהודה holds it is a sign.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives רבה's answer to the question from step 15. He explains the argument without running into that question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question in step 15 only works against someone who holds both that a trampled sign does not count and that people pass over food. רבה holds that people do not pass over food, so that question does not touch him. For רבה, the whole argument between the תנאים is only about a סימן הבא מאליו, a sign that came by accident.

keyTerms.meaning: And רבה would say to you: he would explain it his own way
A sign likely to be trampled, which will probably be ruined by people walking on it
People do not walk past food lying on the ground without picking it up
A sign that came by itself, by accident, and not one the owner made

phrases.english: And Rabba would say to you:
Everyone agrees that a sign likely to be trampled
is not a sign,
and people do not pass over food.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָכָא בְּסִימָן הַבָּא מֵאֵילָיו קָא מִיפַּלְגִי,
phrases.english: And here they argue about a sign that comes by itself.
The first Tanna holds:

phrases.aramaic: סִימָן הַבָּא מֵאֵילָיו – לָא הָוֵי סִימָן,
phrases.english: a sign that comes by itself is not a sign,
and Rabbi Yehuda holds: it is a sign.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives רבה's explanation alongside רב זביד's answer in step 16, within the second version.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Moves the argument to a different kind of sign, so the question in step 15 does not apply
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The question was that the תנא קמא might hold that a trampled sign does not count and that people pass over food, which makes the announcing of loaves hard to explain.
steps.terutzMaskana: For רבה, people do not pass over food. So the question from step 15 does not apply, and the argument is only about an accidental sign.
steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to explain the argument. רב זביד says a trampled sign counts and people pass over food. רבה says a trampled sign does not count and people do not pass over food. Both agree the real argument is about a סימן הבא מאליו.

steps.title: The general rule: saying 'woe for my money loss' means giving up hope
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד in the name of רבא: once the owner says 'woe for the money loss,' he has given up hope of getting the item back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבא: the general rule for a lost object is that once the owner says 'woe for my money loss,' he has given up hope on it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new practical statement. It gives a clear sign that tells us when an owner has given up hope on a lost item.
steps.deeperAnalysis: יאוש (giving up hope) happens in the owner's mind, so we need some outward sign of it. The owner's words 'woe for my money loss' show he already counts the item as gone. From that moment he has given up hope on it.

keyTerms.meaning: The general rule of a lost object
Woe for the money loss: the owner sighs over his lost money
He has given up hope (יאוש) of getting it back

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said in the name of Rava:
The general rule of a lost item:
once he says, 'Woe for the money loss,'
phrases.notes: Literally 'woe for the loss of the pocket,' meaning 'there goes my money.'

phrases.english: he has despaired of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא: כְּלָלָא דַּאֲבֵידְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, separate practical rule about יאוש after the argument over signs ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Once an owner says 'woe for my money loss,' he has given up hope on the item.

steps.title: The final ruling on bundles found in public and private places
steps.stepSummary: Bundles found in a public place belong to the finder. In a private place, if they look like they fell, they belong to the finder. If they look like they were put down, he takes them and announces.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רב זביד said in the name of רבא: the הלכה is that bundles found in a public place belong to the finder. In a private place, if they look like they fell, they belong to the finder. If they look like they were placed there, he takes them and announces them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final practical הלכה for finding bundles of grain. The answer depends on where they are found and how they look.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a public place many people pass by, so the owner has given up hope and the finder keeps them. In a private place, bundles that look like they fell also belong to the finder. If they look like they were put down on purpose, the owner may come back for them, so the finder takes them and announces.

keyTerms.meaning: The final ruling, how we act in practice
Bundles (of grain)
A public place where many people pass
A private place where few people pass
Looking like it fell, or looking like it was put down on purpose
He takes it and announces it

phrases.english: And Rav Zevid said in the name of Rava:
The halakha is: bundles in a public place
these are his.
In a private place, if they look like they fell,
these are his;
if they look like they were placed, he takes them and announces.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַב זְבִיד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא: הִלְכְתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second practical ruling from the same רב זביד in the name of רבא.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Bundles in a public place belong to the finder. In a private place they belong to the finder if they look like they fell, but must be announced if they look like they were put down.

steps.title: The ruling applies only to items without a sign
steps.stepSummary: All of the above is only for items without a סימן. If the item has a סימן, the finder must always announce it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both of these rulings are about an item with no סימן. But for an item that has a סימן, it makes no difference whether it is in a public or private place, or whether it looks like it fell or was placed. He must announce it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא limits the ruling it just gave. It says the ruling only covers items with no סימן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without a סימן, the owner cannot prove the item is his, so he gives up hope. That is why place and position decide the case. With a סימן, the owner expects to get it back, so he does not give up hope, and the finder must always announce.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this and that: both rulings just said
It makes no difference
He must announce it

phrases.aramaic: וְזֶה וָזֶה בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ סִימָן,
phrases.english: And both this and that are about an item with no sign,
phrases.notes: 'This and that' means both rulings in step 19: the public place and the private place.

phrases.english: but for an item that has a sign,
it makes no difference whether in a public place
or in a private place,

phrases.aramaic: בֵּין דֶּרֶךְ נְפִילָה וּבֵין דֶּרֶךְ הַנָּחָה –
phrases.english: whether it looks like it fell or like it was placed,
he must announce.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְזֶה וָזֶה בְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ סִימָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Limits the ruling in step 19 to items with no סימן.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: An item with a סימן must always be announced, wherever it is found and however it looks.
steps.whatToRemember: The order is: first check for a סימן. If there is one, always announce. If there is none, look at the place (public or private) and how it looks (fell or put down).
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think a public place always means the finder keeps it. That is only true when the item has no סימן.
